topic: High-ISO noise is mostly a light problem: photon shot noise is Poisson, SNR = sqrt(photons). For equal brightness ISO 6400 collects 64x fewer photons than ISO 100, so signal-to-noise is sqrt(64) = 8x lower (simulated, shot noise only)

youtube.title: Your High-ISO Photos Aren't Noisy Because of ISO (It's Light)
youtube.description:
Noise at high ISO is mostly photon shot noise: light arrives as discrete photons following Poisson statistics, so with N photons the noise is about sqrt(N) and signal-to-noise is about sqrt(N). To keep the same brightness, ISO 6400 needs 64 times less light than ISO 100 (six stops: 2^6 = 64), so signal-to-noise falls by sqrt(64) = 8 in the shot-noise-limited case. The fix is more light: a wider aperture or a longer exposure. The images are a simulation (shot noise only, a dim scene, illustrative photon counts), not real photos; real cameras also add read noise and processing.
#photography #iso #shorts

sources: https://people.csail.mit.edu/fredo/comp-photo-book/02-fundamentals-06-noise-signal-to-noise-ratio-and-dynamic-range.html (photon shot noise is Poisson: variance = mean, sigma = sqrt(N), SNR = sqrt(N); worst in the shadows)
https://www.tucsen.com/learning/photon-shot-noise-in-scientific-imaging-snr/ (photon shot noise grows as the square root of the signal; shot-noise-limited SNR scales as sqrt(Ne))
Check: ISO 100 -> 6400 = 6 stops = 2^6 = 64x; sqrt(64) = 8. Simulation measured SNR 29.95 vs 3.76 (ratio 8.0) at white level with 900 vs 14.06 photons/px; illustrative counts, shot noise only.
